title: Investing In People Is Also Industrial Policy
text:
Investing In People Is Also Industrial Policy

Tilly Zhang

Gavekal Dragonomics | 7 Sep 2026

China’s government is starting to face up to the reality that, after decades of massive expansion of housing, infrastructure and industrial capacity, it is facing diminishing returns on much new investment in physical assets. Official rhetoric in recent months has acknowledged that rapid investment in the past has led to duplication and wasted resources, and neglected other needs. Now, the center is urging a more considered approach that “places greater emphasis on investment quality and overall returns.” An important theme the government is emphasizing as part of this correction is balancing “investing in things” with “investing in people”—a slogan that has been written into the new Five-Year Plan and other authoritative policy documents. What does this new priority really mean?The government is advertising the “investing in people” initiative as including a redirection of public spending to more direct benefits for households. The Ministry of Finance says it is increasing expenditures on public services that support households, like healthcare and social security, and indeed the numbers show spending on those areas is growing faster. Some official commentaries do discuss “investing in people” as a way of boosting household consumption by improving the social safety net and lowering precautionary savings.
